name: Önge
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Dasgupta, D. & Sharma, S. R. (1982) A Handbook of Onge Language (Anthropological Survey of India); also Ganguly 1966 grammar sketch — neither found online

sources.citation: Zamponi, Raoul & Bernard Comrie. 2021. A Grammar of Akajeru. London: UCL Press. (held in sibling folder akaj1239)
sources.note: Sec. 2.2 p.22 statement (non-phonemic root-initial stress) is explicitly about the Great Andamanese family only; Onge/Jarawa mentioned only for loanwords. Not applicable to Onge.

sources.citation: Blevins, Juliette. 2007. A long lost sister of Proto-Austronesian? Proto-Ongan, mother of Jarawa and Onge of the Andaman Islands. Oceanic Linguistics 46(1):154-198. doi:10.1353/ol.2007.0015 (author postprint via the Internet Archive)
sources.note: Sec. 2.1 'Synchronic phonology' (pp.160-163) gives Onge/Jarawa inventories, max syllable CVC, Onge words vowel-final, mid-vowel harmony, d~r flapping; no statement of where Onge stress falls. Only mentions of stress are 'unstressed syllables' in connection with Jarawa vowel reduction (p.164) and a diachronic remark that a PON doublet 'appears to correlate with stress' (p.167).

sources.citation: Temple, Richard C. 1903. Census of India 1901, vol. III: The Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Report. Ch. IV 'The Languages'. (archive.org;ernet.dli.2015.55927)
sources.note: p.115 (South Andaman/Bojingiji group section, 'Peculiarities of Speech'): 'Stress in Andamanese is placed on every long vowel, or on the first syllable of the root or stem.' This is a generic remark based on Great Andamanese (Bea etc.) material; the Outer Group (Önge-Jarawa) section pp.117-119 is only a Colebrooke/Portman word list with no prosodic remarks. Not an Önge statement.

sources.citation: Dasgupta, D. & S. R. Sharma. 1982. A Hand Book of Onge Language. Linguistic Series 5. Calcutta: Anthropological Survey of India. (134 pp scan; archive.org item onge-language-a-hand-book-of-gasgupta-sharma; second scan dasgupta-d.-sharma-s.-r.-a-hand-book-of-onge-language, scanned only)
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online; also held in print at Harvard (Tozzer Library (offsite storage), call number OC.IND. D 261 h)
sources.harvard_location: Tozzer Library (offsite storage), call number OC.IND. D 261 h
sources.note: Nothing. Ch.1 'Speech Sounds of Onge' (pp.4-9) is a vowel and consonant inventory with articulatory descriptions only; ch.2 covers word formation (vowel harmony et-/ot-, syllable elision in compound verbs). Whole-book a full-text search for stress/accent: no hits; page scan of pp.4 and 9 checked against the scanned.

sources.citation: Majumder, Arup. 2025. A phonological description of the Onge language of Little Andaman. Journal of Literature, Languages and Linguistics 107:26-35. doi:10.7176/JLLL/106-03 (open access; re-analysis of Ganguly 1966)
sources.note: Explicitly silent: sec. 5.4 p.33 'While the document [Ganguly 1966] provides limited information on prosody (stress, intonation, tone).. without explicit data on stress placement or intonation patterns, any conclusions on Onge prosody remain speculative'; sec. 7 lists suprasegmental features as still undescribed.
sources.venue: Journal of Literature, Languages and Linguistics

sources.citation: Abbi, Anvita. 2016. The languages of the Andaman Islands (sections in Hock, H. H. & E. Bashir eds., The Languages and Linguistics of South Asia: A Comprehensive Guide. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton).
sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.note: Handbook summary of Andamanese (incl. Onge) phonology by the only recent fieldworker; could carry a one-line stress statement.

sources.citation: Abbi, Anvita. 2009. Is Great Andamanese genealogically and typologically distinct from Onge and Jarawa? Language Sciences 31(6):791-812.
sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.locator: sec. 4 'The sound system in three languages', printed p. 797; vowel tables 4-6 on p. 800
sources.note: Typological comparison including phonological features of Onge from Abbi's own fieldwork; may tabulate stress/prosody.

sources.citation: Blevins, Juliette. 2009. Andamanese prehistory (ms./paper held in sibling folder akaj1239)
sources.note: Stress remark concerns Aka-Bea only (Man 1923, 'does not appear to be predictable'); nothing on Onge stress.

sources.citation: Burenhult, Niclas. 1996. Deep linguistic prehistory with particular reference to Andamanese. Lund University Dept. of Linguistics Working Papers 45:5-24.
sources.note: Morphosyntactic typology (Nichols-style) from published Onge data; nothing on stress. Bibliography names Nigam 'Report on field investigations on Onge speech (1955-56)' Bull. AnSI 12(3-4):127-45 and Ganguly 1972[1966] Bull. AnSI 15(1-4):1-30.

sources.citation: Brown, A. R. [Radcliffe-Brown]. 1914. Notes on the languages of the Andaman Islands. Anthropos 9:36-52. (archive.org anthropos_1914_9)
sources.note: Transcription note (p.37) and Little Andaman (Önge) grammatical notes on stems/prefixes; no accent or stress statement anywhere in the article (a full-text search for stress/accent/stress: none).

sources.citation: Portman, M. V. 1887. A Manual of the Andamanese Languages. London: W. H. Allen. (DLI scan, archive.org dli.ministry.04152)
sources.note: Introductory grammar (pp.1-8) gives only an alphabet/pronunciation key and word-formation notes for the Great Andamanese languages; Önge words merely added to the lists; no accent statement (only 'prolonged enunciation of one of its syllables' for intensification, p.2, not Önge-specific).

sources.citation: Abbi, Anvita. 2006. Endangered Languages of the Andaman Islands. LINCOM Studies in Asian Linguistics 64. München: LINCOM Europa (ix+175 pp + CD-ROM; ISBN 9783895868665), ch.5 'Lost in the Jungle. The Onge Language'.
